title: The Quiet Room
brief: Six people sat in the dark at 85 Sodela Walk on Thursday evening to speak with the dead. When the lamp came back up, Ottoline Frayne was still in her chair with her eyes open and her heart stopped. The doctor at the table signed her off as heart failure inside the hour, which is very quick work, and her solicitor would like a second opinion. Four addresses. Three days. Everything you need is inside them, and one of the six people at that table is lying to you about something that has nothing to do with the murder.

suspects.name: Dr. Emmanuel Vane
suspects.summary: Attended Ottoline Frayne for eleven years and sat at her right hand on Thursday. Signed the certificate himself, which is permitted, and unusual.
suspects.alibi: Seated at the table throughout, holding the hands of the sitters either side of him. Both confirm it. Neither could see a thing.

suspects.name: Madame Sabine Roux
suspects.summary: Sells contact with the dead at two guineas a sitting. Has been cautioned twice for obtaining money by deception and is unbothered by having been.
suspects.alibi: In the dark, speaking in a voice not her own, with a room full of people listening to her do it.

suspects.name: Gilbert Frayne
suspects.summary: Inherits the house, the annuity, and a debt of his own that has been growing since the spring. Was at the table because his aunt insisted.
suspects.alibi: At the table. Complained loudly throughout about the cold and the nonsense, which several sitters remember, because he would not stop.

motives.label: To close an account
motives.description: Somebody had been taking money from Ottoline Frayne for years and she had finally started counting.

motives.label: The inheritance
motives.description: The house on Sodela Walk and four hundred a year go to the nephew, and the nephew is owed money by men who do not write letters.

motives.label: To avoid exposure
motives.description: A fraud only works while the mark believes. Ottoline Frayne had begun to ask sharper questions than a believer asks.

clues.title: Ottoline Frayne, in her chair
clues.body: Upright, hands still resting on the table where the circle had joined them, eyes open. No mark on her, no disorder to her clothes, nothing knocked over. A woman of sixty-eight whose heart stopped is not remarkable. A woman of sixty-eight whose heart stopped while she was holding two people's hands, in a room nobody left, is a different matter.

clues.title: A cup at her place
clues.body: Bone china, a mouthful of cold tea still in the bottom. Madame Roux serves tea before every sitting; it settles the nerves, she says, and the sitters are grateful for it. Five cups were cleared and washed on Thursday night. This one was not, because it had rolled under the fringe of the cloth.

clues.title: Analysis of the dregs
clues.body: Digitalis. Not a trace of it either — the residue in a mouthful of tea puts the dose at something near four times what a physician would ever write for a woman her age. Digitalis is a heart medicine. In this quantity it is a heart stopper, and it works within the hour, and it leaves a body looking exactly like heart failure.

clues.title: Eleven minutes of dark
clues.body: Madame Roux is precise about it, because the timing is her craft: the lamp goes out and stays out for eleven minutes while she works. Nobody can see anything. Nobody can be seen. She offers this freely, and only afterwards seems to hear what she has said.

clues.title: The prescription book
clues.body: Vane's own hand, his own book. Ottoline Frayne, a fresh bottle of digitalis issued on the Monday — three days before she died — at twice the strength of every bottle he had written her for eleven years. There is no note explaining the change. She was not seen at the practice that week.

clues.title: The Frayne accounts
clues.body: Ottoline Frayne kept her own books in a small hard hand. Under the heading DR. VANE — CONSULTATIONS she had gone back seven years and totalled what she had paid against the dates she could actually remember being ill. The two columns are three hundred and forty pounds apart. The last entry is dated the Tuesday. Beside it she has written: ask him Thursday.

clues.title: The will
clues.body: The house, the contents, and four hundred a year to Gilbert Frayne, sole surviving relative. Drawn up nine years ago and never altered. He knew, everybody knew, and he had been waiting long enough that another year would hardly have killed him.

clues.title: How the trick is done
clues.body: She admits the lot without much prompting, and with something close to pride: the darkness, the voice, the cold draught from a cracked sash, the details gathered beforehand from servants and handbags and the way a person's face moves when you guess near. Every word of the seance is a fraud. She has never once spoken to the dead, and she would like it noted that she has never once killed anybody either.

clues.title: An unsigned note
clues.body: Found in Ottoline Frayne's writing case, in a hand that is not hers: You are being taken for a fool and you will not be told twice. No date, no signature, no envelope. It could have been written by anyone who had been in that room, which is the trouble with it.

clues.title: A pawn ticket
clues.body: Made out to G. Frayne, Tuesday of last week, against a gold hunter watch. Eleven pounds. The broker remembers him because he asked twice whether the ticket could be made out in another name, and was told twice that it could not.

clues.title: What the nephew says
clues.body: He does not pretend to have loved her and he does not pretend he is sorry about the money. He says he sat through eleven minutes of a woman putting on a voice while his aunt held his hand, and that her hand was warm the whole time, and then the lamp came up and it was not. He says it too plainly to be performing.

clues.title: The coroner's marginal note
clues.body: The certificate says heart failure and the coroner has accepted it, because a physician who was present signed it. But somebody in that office has pencilled in the margin, in a hand that is not the coroner's: no post-mortem requested by family. Attending phys. also certifying. Query.

questions.answer: "Six sitters. Tea at eight, because a nervous room hears nothing. Lamp out at a quarter past." She lays it out like a recipe, unembarrassed. "Eleven minutes in the dark. I am precise about that — less and they are not ready, more and somebody laughs. When the lamp came up she was as you found her."

questions.text: None of it is real, is it.
questions.answer: "Not a word." She says it the way another woman might admit to dyeing her hair. "The voice, the draught, the cold hand on the shoulder. I learn what they want to hear before they arrive and I give it to them, and they go home comforted, and I am two guineas better off. I am a liar, Mr. Investigator. I am not a poisoner. Those are quite different trades."

She stops moving for the first time. "I pour six and set them at the places. Then I am at the sideboard with my back to the room for a minute, perhaps two, while they settle themselves." A pause. "Anyone at that table could have reached her cup. Anyone at all. I had not thought of it in those terms until this moment."

questions.text: You inherit. Let us start there.
questions.answer: "I do. Four hundred a year and a cold house, and I shan't pretend to be sorry about it." He meets your eye, which the guilty rarely manage this early. "I held her hand for eleven minutes in the dark while that woman put on a voice. It was warm the whole time. Then the lamp came up and it wasn't. Make of that what you like."

questions.text: You certified a death you were present at.
questions.answer: "It is entirely permitted, and I have done it perhaps forty times." He is unruffled and he keeps his hands still, which is itself a decision. "She had a weak heart for a decade. She was seized by a foolish entertainment in an overheated room. There is no mystery here except the one the solicitor is paying you to manufacture."

questions.text: You doubled her digitalis on the Monday. Why?
questions.answer: For the first time the hands move. "Her symptoms had worsened. I adjusted the dose." — She was not seen at the practice that week. — "I adjusted it on the basis of eleven years of knowing the woman." He stands, and the interview is over, and the answer to the only question that mattered is that he does not have one.

locations.description: Your own two rooms above the tobacconist. The solicitor's letter is on the desk with a cheque clipped to it, and the cheque is smaller than the letter suggests.

85 Sodela Walk. Madame Roux takes the ground floor: a parlour with the curtains permanently drawn, a round table, six chairs, and a sash window that does not quite close. Ottoline Frayne's chair has not been moved. Gilbert Frayne is here too, waiting for somebody to release the house to him.

Petrakis Medical Clinic, where Dr. Vane keeps consulting rooms three days a week. Waiting chairs, a locked dispensary, and a prescription book on the desk that he has not thought to move, because he does not believe anyone will ask.

The Blue Dollar Apartments, where Ottoline Frayne actually lived — two doors from the seance she attended every Thursday. Her writing case is on the bureau and her account books are in it, kept in a hand so small and hard you need the lamp to read them.
Marlowe Loan & Pawn. Wedding rings under glass, a broker who remembers every face, and a ledger he will let you see if you are pleasant about it.

tutorial.title: Get to the scene
tutorial.body:
The map is the board. Every gold pin is somewhere you can go, and there are over a thousand of them — most have nothing to do with this. Click a pin to read it, then DRIVE OVER to move the team there.

Go to 85 Sodela Walk, in Cherwood. Travel costs hours, and hours are all you have.

tutorial.title: Turn the room over
tutorial.body:
SEARCH the place you are standing in. It costs hours whether you find anything or not — that is the whole game, and it is why you cannot search all thousand pins.

Search the parlour.

tutorial.title: Talk to somebody
tutorial.body:
People are at locations, not on a list. Madame Roux is in this room. Ask her a question — it is cheaper than a search, and some questions only unlock once you hold the right evidence.

Ask her about Thursday evening.

tutorial.title: Send something away
tutorial.body:
Some evidence can go to the laboratory. It is the most expensive action in the game and you will rarely afford more than one or two, so choose carefully.

You found a cup that was never washed. Send it to the lab.

tutorial.title: Name them
tutorial.body:
That is every action in the game: travel, search, interview, lab, accuse. The rest is yours.

When you are ready, ACCUSE — you must name a person, a reason, and three pieces of evidence that prove it. You get one attempt. Nobody will tell you when you are ready.

solution.epilogue:
Eleven years of consultations she never had, three hundred and forty pounds, and an old woman patient enough to go back through seven years of her own housekeeping to prove it. She wrote ask him Thursday in her account book on the Tuesday, and on the Thursday she sat down at a round table with him and put her hand in his.

He did not need the dark. That was the elegant part, and it is what nearly worked: the dark made everyone look at Sabine Roux, and Sabine Roux was a proven liar with a room full of people watching her lie. But the digitalis was in the cup before the lamp ever went out, and it was in the cup because Vane had spent the previous three days making sure Ottoline Frayne had a bottle at home that was strong enough to explain the dose if anybody ever checked. He wrote her a prescription she never asked for, so that her own medicine cabinet would testify for him.

He is struck off in the spring and hanged in the summer. Sabine Roux is fined nine pounds for obtaining money by deception, pays it in cash, and is sitting six people at the round table again by August. Gilbert Frayne gets the house, sells it inside a month, and is in debt again by the following spring.
solution.failureEpilogue:
Dr. Vane attends the inquest, gives his evidence in a calm and professional manner, and is thanked by the coroner for his trouble. The prescription book stays on his desk for another week and then it does not. There is no post-mortem, because the family did not request one, because the family is a nephew who wanted the house and got it.

Somewhere in the account books at the Blue Dollar Apartments there are two columns three hundred and forty pounds apart, and a line in a small hard hand that reads ask him Thursday, and nobody reads it again. Vane moves his practice to Cherwood the following year and does rather well there.
